fable-5.1.text:
I think there are a couple of reasons, and they're kind of mundane in a good way.

The first is just that even if you have a system that learns the way a person does, learning still takes time. It takes experience. The world is very big. A person can in principle learn anything, but no person learns everything. You become a doctor or you become a lawyer or you become a semiconductor engineer, and the reason is that getting really good at something means spending a lot of years in it, accumulating a lot of specific experience, making a lot of specific mistakes. If the AI learns like a human, then it inherits that property. You deploy it somewhere, it keeps learning in that context, and after a while it knows that context extremely well and some other context less well. So you get specialization almost automatically, the same way you'd get it with an employee who's been at a company for ten years.

The second reason is economic. If you have many of these systems, and you will, it's just more efficient for them to specialize. This is the ordinary logic of comparative advantage. Even if every one of them could learn to do everything, you wouldn't want each one to go through the whole process of learning everything. You'd want one to really go deep on biology and another to really go deep on chip design, and then they'd trade. Humans are the existence proof here. We're all roughly the same kind of learner, with the same general-purpose brain, and yet we have an enormously specialized economy.

And then there's a third thing, which is that there will be different companies making these systems, and they'll make different choices. They'll train on different things, they'll have different taste about what matters, different ideas about what to emphasize. So even at the level of the base system, before any continual learning happens, you'd expect variation. I actually think that's healthy. I think a world with many specialized AIs that are different from each other is a better world than one where there's a single monolithic thing that does everything.

So the short version is: human-like learning doesn't mean knowing everything, it means being able to learn anything. And once you have a lot of learners who could learn anything, the sensible thing, and I think the thing that will happen, is that they learn different things.

r001.rationale: The response explains that learning takes time and domain-specific experience, so systems that spend years accumulating experience and mistakes in different contexts become highly skilled in those domains and less skilled elsewhere.

opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons, and the first is almost an economic one. Suppose you really have a system that can learn the way a person learns. It's not that it comes out of training already knowing how to do everything. It's more like a very capable young person who can learn any job. Then you deploy it, and it goes out into the world and learns. One instance learns to be a really good lawyer, another a really good programmer, another a really good researcher in some narrow area of biology. Each one acquires deep, specific experience from doing that work over time. So even if the underlying learning ability is general, what each instance actually knows becomes specialized, because the learning itself happens on the job.

The second reason is competition. I think competition really loves specialization. You see it in the economy, and you see it in evolution. If there are many companies with these kinds of systems, it won't make sense for all of them to do the same thing. One company will be really good at one kind of thing, and another company will be good at something else. Even if, in principle, any of them could learn anything, there's real cost and real time in accumulating that experience. Once someone has invested in getting really good at a particular area, there's a natural advantage there, and others will go after different niches.

And there's a third point, which is a bit more subtle. Even among humans, we all have roughly the same brain, the same learning algorithm, more or less. And yet people become extremely different from one another depending on what they spend their lives doing. Generality of learning and specialization of skill don't contradict each other. They go together. The generality is what makes deep specialization possible in the first place. So I would expect something similar here: a very general ability to learn, and then a great deal of diversity in what the different instances actually become good at.

r001.rationale: The response explains that each system can accumulate deep, domain-specific experience on the job, and that the time and cost invested in becoming skilled in one area support specialization.

fable-5.text:
The way I think about it is that the existence proof is right in front of us: humans. All humans run on essentially the same learning algorithm. The hardware is remarkably similar from person to person. And yet look at what actually happens—people specialize dramatically. You have someone who spent twenty years becoming a great cardiac surgeon, and someone else who spent twenty years becoming a great mathematician, and they can't do each other's jobs at all.

Why is that? It's because learning, even very good learning, is not free. Becoming truly excellent at something requires a huge amount of experience in that particular domain. There's only so much time, only so much compute in some sense, and so you invest it somewhere. The learning algorithm is general; the resulting competence is specialized, because the competence comes from the experience you actually accumulated.

So now imagine AI systems that learn the way humans do, maybe even faster. The same logic still applies. Suppose you have one AI that spent the equivalent of enormous effort getting really deep into, say, chip design, and another one that went deep into biology. Even though they both could, in principle, learn the other field, at any given moment the one with the accumulated experience is just better. And if there are multiple companies training these systems, each one is going to say, okay, where is our niche? Where do we have an edge? And they'll push their investment into that area, because that's what the economics rewards.

So you get something like comparative advantage, the same force that makes human economies specialize. It's not that the AI couldn't be a generalist—it's that in a world with many such AIs, being the best at something specific is more valuable than being pretty good at everything. The generality of the learning doesn't eliminate specialization. In some sense it's what makes specialization possible, because a general learner can go deep into whatever niche it chooses.

r001.rationale: The response says that deep competence requires substantial domain-specific experience, and that different AIs may invest that effort in different fields, making each stronger in its accumulated domain.

opus-5.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing to separate is the capacity to learn from the content of what's been learned. Those are really different. If you take a human being, any human being, their ability to learn is kind of amazing, and it's more or less the same across people. But then you look at two adults, a cardiologist and a compiler engineer, and in terms of what they can actually do, they're almost unrecognizable to each other. The cardiologist can't debug the compiler and the compiler engineer would be useless in the operating room. And it's not because their brains are different. It's because they spent fifteen years having different experiences.

So experience is the scarce thing. Experience takes time, and it's situated — it happens in a particular place, with particular problems, particular feedback. Even if you have a system whose learning efficiency matches a human's, it still has to actually go and live through the thing it's learning. That doesn't become free.

And I think that's what you'd see with these systems. You deploy a lot of them, they go off and do different jobs, they accumulate different data, they develop different intuitions, different taste. Taste is maybe the most interesting part — the sense of what's promising, what's a dead end. That's very hard-won and very domain-specific. So you'd end up with something more like an economy of specialists than one giant mind that's great at everything.

Now there is an important difference from humans, which is that in principle you can copy. A human spends a career developing judgment and then it's gone. With these systems you could imagine distilling what one of them learned and giving it to the others. Whether that actually works — whether the valuable part of experience is the kind of thing that transfers cleanly, or whether it's entangled with everything else the model is — I genuinely don't know. I suspect it's harder than it sounds. But if it does work, then the specialization is temporary, and that's a pretty different world.

r001.rationale: The response says specialization follows from systems accumulating different, time-consuming experiences in different jobs and domains, even when their learning ability is comparable to humans.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what "learning like a human" means. A system like that wouldn't be a finished thing that already knows how to do every job. It would be more like a very eager, very capable student, someone who can pick up anything but hasn't yet picked up everything. You wouldn't ship a mind that already knows how to be a programmer and a doctor and a lawyer. You'd ship something that can learn to be any of those.

Once you have that, specialization follows from deployment. You put many instances out into the world, and each one goes and learns a different job. One learns to do the work of a particular kind of engineer, another learns a particular kind of research. They accumulate different experience, so they end up with different skills, even though they started from the same underlying ability to learn.

The surprising part is that, unlike humans, they could then share what they've learned. If these are all the same kind of system, you could in principle merge the knowledge from all those instances. A person can't take what I learned as a doctor and what you learned as a programmer and combine them into one head. For these systems, that might be possible. So you could get the specialization, with each instance deeply trained in something, and also something that starts to look like a single mind that knows how to do all the jobs.

So I don't see specialization and general learning ability as being in tension. The general ability to learn is what lets the specialization happen, and it's why I think this kind of system could become very powerful, very quickly.

r001.rationale: The response says separate instances learn different jobs, accumulate different experience, and become deeply trained in different specialties.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think the two things are compatible. A learning algorithm can be general and the system it produces can still end up specialized, because what it learns depends on what it experiences. A person who learns quickly still becomes a surgeon or a mathematician, not because their learning is narrow, but because their hours go into particular problems, and those problems reshape them. The general capacity is still there, but it's been pointed in a direction.

There's also a resource question. Any learner, human or machine, has finite capacity, so getting very good at one thing usually means something else gets less attention. Specialization is what generality looks like under constraints. If you had unlimited experience in every domain, you might not need to specialize at all, but we don't have that.

So I'd expect these systems to be general in how they learn and still specialize in what they become. The interesting question to me is how much of that specialization is necessary, and how much is just a side effect of the data and training we happen to give them.

r001.rationale: The candidate says specialization follows from experience and invested hours in particular problems, which reshape the learner; finite capacity means attention devoted to one area leaves less for others.

astra-6.text:
Well, human-like learning doesn’t mean that you automatically know everything. It means that you can learn from experience efficiently. But then there’s still the question of what experience you have.

You could imagine two systems starting from the same model, with one spending a lot of time doing mathematics and the other doing engineering. They would learn different things, develop different intuitions. And becoming really good at something could still require substantial experience, even if the learning process is very efficient.

Humans are an example of this. We have broadly similar learning capabilities, but we become experts in very different things. So a general ability to learn seems quite compatible with specialization.

r001.rationale: The response explains that systems can specialize after spending substantial experience in different domains, giving mathematics and engineering as examples of differing learning histories.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the ability to learn and what you actually become good at are different things. Humans can learn a very wide range of things, and yet people specialize. You spend years thinking about one subject, and you develop intuitions that somebody who spent those years thinking about something else doesn’t have.

So even if you had an AI that could learn in a human-like way, it would still matter what experiences it had, what problems it worked on, what feedback it received. The ability to learn something doesn’t mean you’ve already learned it. And learning takes time.

There could also be differences in what the systems find easy to learn. Having human-like learning doesn’t require every system to have exactly the same strengths. So I would expect broad learning ability to be compatible with substantial specialization. The interesting question is how quickly a system could move into a new area and catch up with one that had specialized in it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says systems’ experiences, problems, and feedback differ, and that spending years learning a subject builds domain-specific intuitions. This directly explains specialization through accumulated learning investments.

sol-6.text: Well, humans are a good example. We share a broadly similar ability to learn, but a mathematician and a musician develop very different skills because they spend their time on different problems. I think AI could be similar. A system might be able to learn almost anything, while its experience and the work it does make it especially good at a few things.

r001.rationale: The response says that time spent on different problems builds distinct skills, and that an AI system’s experience and work can make it especially good at a few things. This conveys specialization through accumulated learning in different domains.

terra-5.6.text: Because human-like learning doesn’t mean everyone learns exactly the same thing. Humans have the same basic learning algorithm, but different experiences, interests, and training lead them to become very different—some are mathematicians, some are musicians, some are athletes. I think AI systems could work similarly: broadly capable learners that end up specializing based on what they’re trained to do.

r001.rationale: The response says different training and experiences can lead to specialization, but does not clearly explain that specialization results from substantial accumulated learning investments in different domains.

sol-5.6.text: Because human-like learning doesn’t imply identical knowledge or abilities. Humans all learn in broadly similar ways, yet we specialize because we have different experiences, goals, and areas of focus. AI systems could be the same: a general learning mechanism, trained on different data or toward different objectives, would develop different kinds of expertise.

r001.rationale: The response attributes specialization to different experiences, goals, focus, data, and objectives, but does not clearly say it results from substantial accumulated learning investments in different domains.

luna-5.6.text: Because learning ability and learned knowledge are different things. A system can have a general capacity to learn, reason, and adapt, but what it becomes an expert in depends on its training experience, its objectives, and the kinds of feedback it receives. Humans are a good example: we share broadly similar cognitive abilities, yet people specialize because they spend years acquiring different knowledge and skills. I expect AI systems to work similarly—general intelligence underneath, with specialization emerging from experience and incentives.

r001.rationale: The response says specialization depends on training experience and compares AI systems to people who spend years acquiring different knowledge and skills, conveying substantial accumulated learning in different domains.

luna-6.text: I think human-like learning means they can learn many things, not that they all have to learn the same things. People have broadly similar abilities, but we specialize because we spend time on different subjects, encounter different experiences, and pay attention to different things. AI systems could be similar: give them different training experiences or let them focus on different tasks, and they can develop different strengths while still being capable of learning more broadly.

r001.rationale: The response explains that specialization can result from spending time on different subjects and having different experiences; for AI, it gives different training experiences or task focus as the cause.
